source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. X (Montreuil)

1.title: Elucidatio capituli primi: Onus quod vidit Habacuc propheta.
1.title_en: Explanation of the first chapter: The burden that Habacuc the prophet saw.

paras.t: HABACUC prophetasse post duarum tribuum captivitatem a Chaldæis, constat ex eo quod in Daniele habetur, quemadmodum angelus Domini apparuit Habacuc in Judæa, eique jussit ferre prandium quod paravit, Danieli in Babylone, qui erat in lacu leonum. Quemadmodum autem Nahum vaticinatus est contra Niniven atque Assyrios decem tribuum vastatores, sic Habacuc prophetavit contra Babylonem et Chaldæos duarum tribuum oppressores.
paras.en: That Habacuc prophesied after the captivity of the two tribes by the Chaldeans is clear from what is found in Daniel: how the angel of the Lord appeared to Habacuc in Judea and bade him carry the dinner he had prepared to Daniel in Babylon, who was in the lions' den[[Dan 14:33||]]. And as Nahum prophesied against Ninive and the Assyrians, the destroyers of the ten tribes, so Habacuc prophesied against Babylon and the Chaldeans, the oppressors of the two tribes.

paras.t: Ponens ergo Habacuc titulum sive proœmium, tangit voluminis sui materiam, dicens : Onus, id est pondus miseriæ seu gravis punitio Chaldæorum, quod vidit, id est, in spiritu præcognovit, Habacuc propheta. In quo patet Montani insania, asserentis Prophetas non intellexisse quid dicerent, sed sine mente strepitum vocis cum irrationali excessu formasse. Denique tres Prophetæ sunt, quorum exordium est, Onus, videlicet Nahum, Habacuc, Malachias.
paras.en: Setting down, then, a title or preface, Habacuc touches on the matter of his volume, saying: [[1:1|The burden|Onus]], that is, the weight of misery, or the heavy punishment of the Chaldeans, [[1:1|that|quod]] [[1:1|Habakkuk the prophet|Habacuc propheta]] [[1:1|saw|vidit]], that is, foreknew in the spirit. Herein the madness of Montanus is plain [the second-century heresiarch, who held that the prophet speaks in ecstasy, out of his senses], who asserted that the Prophets did not understand what they were saying, but without the mind formed the sound of the voice in an irrational transport. Lastly, there are three Prophets whose opening is *The burden*, namely Nahum, Habacuc and Malachias.

paras.t: Proœmio posito, incipit Propheta tractatum a querela, quæstione, seu oratione implicita. Usquequo, Domine, clamabo, et non exaudies ? Primo elucidanda sunt verba ista ad litteram, deinde generalius exponentur, secundum mysticum intellectum.
paras.en: The preface set down, the Prophet begins his treatise with a complaint, a question, or a prayer implied in them: [[1:2|How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear?|Usquequo, Domine, clamabo, et non exaudies]] First these words are to be explained according to the letter; then they will be expounded more generally, according to the mystical sense.

paras.t: Considerans ergo sanctus vir impiissimorum Chaldæorum prosperitatem et violentiam, Judæorum vero calamitatem et oppressionem, prorumpit in dolorosam et piam querelam vel quæstionem, quæ tamen per modum orationis accipi potest, ut quum ait Psalmista : Usquequo, Domine, oblivisceris me in finem ? usquequo avertis faciem tuam a me ? Ait itaque in persona sua ac Judæorum, ad Deum pro liberatione a Chaldæis clamantium : Usquequo Domine, clamabo, affectuose orando pro liberatione a Babylonica captivitate ? vociferabor ad te, id est, ardentissime te precabor, vim patiens, id est, violentiam sustinens a Chaldæis, et non salvabis te invocantes ? tanquam dicat, Diu differs.
paras.en: Considering, then, the prosperity and violence of the most impious Chaldeans, and the calamity and oppression of the Jews, the holy man breaks out into a sorrowful and devout complaint or question, which may nevertheless be taken as a prayer, as when the Psalmist says: [[Ps 12:1|How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me unto the end? how long dost thou turn away thy face from me?|Usquequo, Domine, oblivisceris me in finem ? usquequo avertis faciem tuam a me]] He says, therefore, in his own person and in that of the Jews crying to God for deliverance from the Chaldeans: [[1:2|How long, O Lord, shall I cry|Usquequo Domine, clamabo]], praying with all my heart for deliverance from the Babylonian captivity? [[1:2|shall I cry out to thee|vociferabor ad te]], that is, shall I beseech thee most ardently, [[1:2|suffering violence|vim patiens]], that is, enduring violence from the Chaldeans, [[1:2|and thou wilt not save|et non salvabis]] those who call upon thee? As if he should say: Thou delayest long.

paras.t: Quare ostendisti mihi iniquitatem ? Secundum Hieronymum, nullus Prophetarum tam audaci voce ausus est Deum ad disceptationem justitiæ provocare, cur in rebus humanis et mundi istius pompa, tanta rerum versetur iniquitas. Causatur enim quodammodo contra Deum, et ait : Quare ostendisti mihi iniquitatem ? id est, cur ad hoc deductus sum, et tam diu vixi, vel, cur me sciente aut cognoscente, factum est istud, videlicet, ut viderem iniquitatem et crudelitatem Nabuchodonosor et Chaldæorum contra regnum Juda et templum? Et laborem videre, quem populus tuus sustinuit, tribulantibus eos Chaldæis, prædam et injustitiam contra me, id est Judæorum spoliationem et injuriosam calumniam qua a Babyloniis pressi sunt. Quamvis autem Judæi Deo volente puniebantur, et juste, tamen Chaldæi fecerunt hoc crudeliter et injuste, videlicet impia voluntate et intentione superba. Vel Propheta dicit hoc in persona sui ac innocentium Judæorum, a Chaldæis injuriam perpessorum.
paras.en: [[1:3|Why hast thou shewn me iniquity|Quare ostendisti mihi iniquitatem]]? According to Jerome, none of the Prophets dared with so bold a voice to challenge God to a debate on justice, asking why, in human affairs and in the pomp of this world, so great iniquity holds sway. For he in a manner pleads a case against God, and says: [[1:3|Why hast thou shewn me iniquity|Quare ostendisti mihi iniquitatem]]? that is, why have I been brought to this, and lived so long? or, why has this come about with my knowledge and awareness, namely that I should see the iniquity and cruelty of Nabuchodonosor and of the Chaldeans against the kingdom of Juda and the temple? [[1:3|and grievance, to see|Et laborem videre]] [*laborem*, "labour, toil"], namely the toil which thy people endured while the Chaldeans afflicted them, [[1:3|rapine and injustice before me|prædam et injustitiam contra me]] [*contra me*, literally "against me"], that is, the plundering of the Jews, and the wrongful oppression by which they were pressed by the Babylonians. Now although the Jews were being punished by God's will, and justly, yet the Chaldeans did this cruelly and unjustly, that is, with an impious will and a proud intention. Or else the Prophet says this in his own person and in that of the innocent Jews who suffered wrong from the Chaldeans.

paras.t: Porro, secundum Hieronymum, Bedam, et Glossam, ista et item verba sequentia accipi possunt, non quasi in persona Prophetæ, sed imperfectorum prolata, ignorantium electos in sæculo isto per tribulationes purgari, quemadmodum aurum igne probatur. Alii quidam affirmant hæc dici in persona perfectorum, divini judicii profunditatem stupentium, justoque zelo contra iniquos zelantium. — Est ergo pensandum, quod verba ista accipi possunt per modum querelæ et quæstionis, ex impatientia et ignorantia procedentis: sicque conveniunt imperfectis, qui non attendunt investigabilia judicia Dei, altitudinemque divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ ejus, qui non ita videt et judicat sicut homo, sed propter causas sibi notas permittit electos calumniari, nec ad votum eos exaudit. Quemadmodum si ægrotus et febribus æstuans, aquam frigidam quærat a medico, dicens : Vim patior, excrucior, uror : usquequo clamabo, o medice, et non exaudies ? Cui respondet sapientissimus et clementissimus medicus : Scio quando dandum est quod petis; non miserebor modo, quoniam misericordia ista esset crudelitas, et voluntas tua contra te petit. Pariformiter Deus omnipotens sciens clementiæ suæ pondus atque mensuram, crebro non exaudit clamantem ad votum, ut probet, et ad instantiores preces provocet eum, et quasi in igne excoctum, puriorem reddat ac justiorem. — Secundo accipi possunt hæc verba ad modum interrogationis, ex zelo justitiæ et doloris abundantia procedentis, atque ex quadam familiaritate fiduciaque ad Deum, ad provocandum misericordiam ejus : sicque conveniunt viris perfectis.
paras.en: Further, according to Jerome, Bede and the Gloss, these words, and likewise those that follow, can be taken as spoken not in the person of the Prophet but in that of the imperfect, who do not know that the elect are purged in this world by tribulations, as gold is proved by fire[[Wis 3:6||]]. Certain others affirm that these things are said in the person of the perfect, who stand amazed at the depth of the divine judgment, and burn with a just zeal against the wicked. — It is to be considered, then, that these words can be taken by way of a complaint and question proceeding from impatience and ignorance; and so they befit the imperfect, who do not attend to the unsearchable judgments of God, and to [[Rom 11:33|the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge|altitudinemque divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ]] of him who does not see and judge as man does[[1 Kings 16:7||]], but for causes known to himself permits the elect to be wronged, and does not hear them as they would wish. It is as if a sick man, burning with fever, should ask the physician for cold water, saying: I suffer violence, I am tormented, I burn: how long shall I cry, O physician, and thou wilt not hear? And the most wise and most merciful physician answers him: I know when what thou askest should be given; I will not have pity now, because that pity would be cruelty, and thy will asks against thyself. In like manner almighty God, knowing the weight and measure of his clemency, often does not hear one who cries to him as he would wish, so as to try him, and to stir him to more urgent prayers, and, as though refining him in the fire, to make him purer and more just. — Secondly, these words can be taken by way of a question proceeding from zeal for justice and an abundance of grief, and from a certain familiarity and confidence towards God, so as to move his mercy; and so they befit perfect men.

paras.t: Quare respicis per exhibitionem beneficiorum tuorum, id est, clementer et patienter attendis, contemptores, id est Chaldæos idola venerantes, et Deum verum spernentes, et taces, id est, non vindicas statim, nec redarguis, conculcante impio justiorem se, id est, rege et populo Babylonis Judaicam plebem, in qua aliqui justi fuerunt? Huic querelæ quæstionique Habacuc, simile est illud Jeremiæ : Justus quidem tu es, Domine, si disputem tecum; verumtamen justa loquar ad te : Quare via impiorum prosperatur, et bene est omnibus qui prævaricantur et inique agunt? Illud quoque Job : Numquid contra Deum disputatio mea est, ut merito non debeam contristari? Quare ergo impii vivunt, sublevati sunt, confortatique divitiis? Et facies homines quasi pisces maris, et quasi reptilia non habentia ducem, id est, sine cura et providentia eos permittes, ut irrationalia, in quibus majora devorant minora, nec infertur a te illis vindicta. Istud in persona perfectorum non dicitur asserative, sed quia secundum exteriorem superficiem sic esse videtur. Nec sic intelligendum est, quod irrationalia non cadant sub providentia Dei, quum ipsi sit cura de omnibus, ut dicitur in libro Sapientiæ; dicatque Salvator : Respicite volatilia cœli, quoniam non serunt neque metunt, et Pater vester cœlestis pascit ea; alibi quoque : Nonne quinque passeres veneunt dipondio, et unus ex illis non est in oblivione coram Deo? Sed ideo ista dicuntur, quoniam rationalium creaturarum habet Deus speciali modo curam ac providentiam, eo quod actus earum cadant sub ratione meriti atque demeriti. Sicque dicit Apostolus ad Corinthios : Numquid cura est Deo de bobus?
paras.en: [[1:13|Why lookest thou|Quare respicis]], by bestowing thy benefits, that is, why dost thou regard mercifully and patiently, the despisers [Denis here takes up, ahead of their place, the words of vv. 13–14 in the old reading from the Greek, which has *contemptores*, "despisers", where the Vulgate has "them that do unjust things"; he comes back to them below], that is, the Chaldeans, who worship idols and spurn the true God, [[1:13|and holdest thy peace|et taces]], that is, dost not straightway avenge nor rebuke, while the wicked treadeth down [[1:13|the man that is more just than himself|justiorem se]], that is, while the king and people of Babylon tread down the Jewish people, among whom there were some just men? Like this complaint and question of Habacuc is that of Jeremias: [[Jer 12:1|Thou indeed, O Lord, art just, if I plead with thee, but yet I will speak what is just to thee: Why doth the way of the wicked prosper: why is it well with all them that transgress, and do wickedly?|Justus quidem tu es, Domine, si disputem tecum; verumtamen justa loquar ad te : Quare via impiorum prosperatur, et bene est omnibus qui prævaricantur et inique agunt?]] That of Job also: [[Job 21:4|Is my debate|Numquid]] against God [the Vulgate has "against man"], [[Job 21:4|that I should not have just reason to be troubled?|ut merito non debeam contristari?]] [[Job 21:7|Why then do the wicked live, are they advanced, and strengthened with riches?|Quare ergo impii vivunt, sublevati sunt, confortatique divitiis?]] [[1:14|And thou wilt make men as the fishes of the sea|Et facies homines quasi pisces maris]], [[1:14|and as the creeping things|et quasi reptilia]] that have no leader, that is, thou wilt leave them without care and providence, like brute creatures, among which the greater devour the lesser, and no vengeance is brought upon them by thee. This is said in the person of the perfect not as an assertion, but because on the outward surface it seems to be so. Nor is it to be understood as if brute creatures did not fall under the providence of God, since he has [[Wis 6:8|care of all|cura de omnibus]], as is said in the book of Wisdom; and the Saviour says: [[Matt 6:26|Behold the birds of the air, for they neither sow, nor do they reap|Respicite volatilia cœli, quoniam non serunt neque metunt]], [[Matt 6:26|and your heavenly Father feedeth them|et Pater vester cœlestis pascit ea]]; and elsewhere: [[Luke 12:6|Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God?|Nonne quinque passeres veneunt dipondio, et unus ex illis non est in oblivione coram Deo?]] But these things are said because God has care and providence of rational creatures in a special manner, in that their acts fall under the account of merit and demerit. And so the Apostle says to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 9:9|Doth God take care for oxen?|Numquid cura est Deo de bobus]]

paras.t: Et factum est judicium tale quale, puta perversum : id est, quoniam taces impiis justos calcantibus, ideo judicatur, non secundum veritatem atque justitiam, sed secundum potentiam et perversitatem; et contradictio facta est potentior, id est, negatio veritatis prævaluit æquitati, estque oppressa justitia, quoniam impii non videntes divinae justitiae ultionem, peccant secure. Hoc est quod in Ecclesiaste inducitur : Etenim quia non cito profertur contra malos judicium, absque ullo timore filii hominum perpetrant mala.
paras.en: [[1:3|and there is a judgment|Et factum est judicium]], such as it is, that is, a perverse one: that is, because thou holdest thy peace while the wicked trample on the just, judgment is therefore given not according to truth and justice, but according to power and perversity; [[1:3|but opposition is more powerful|et contradictio facta est potentior]], that is, the denial of the truth has prevailed over equity, and justice is oppressed, because the wicked, not seeing the vengeance of the divine justice, sin without fear. This is what is brought forward in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 8:11|For because sentence is not speedily pronounced against the evil, the children of men commit evils without any fear.|Etenim quia non cito profertur contra malos judicium, absque ullo timore filii hominum perpetrant mala]]

paras.t: Propter hoc lacerata est lex, id est praevaricata ab impiis, quum istud sit contra legem naturalem et scriptam, divinam atque civilem. Potest quoque referri ad destructionem legis Mosaicae, quam laceraverunt Chaldaei, comburendo bibliothecam Judaeorum, quam Esdras postmodum reparavit. Et non pervenit usque ad finem judicium, id est, justum exitum non est sortitum. Finis enim judicii est, ut unusquisque quod promeruit, recipiat, bonus honorem, malus vindictam ; sed propter praedicta oppositum contigit, quantum ad vitam praesentem. Quia impius praevalet adversus justum, puta rex et exercitus Babylonis contra Judaicum populum, in quo quidam justi fuerunt translati captique, ut Daniel, Azarias, Ananias et Misael, atque Ezechiel; propterea egreditur judicium perversum, non a Deo, sed a Chaldaeis contra Judaeos, quos saepe oppresserunt crudeliter.
paras.en: [[1:4|Therefore the law is torn in pieces|Propter hoc lacerata est lex]], that is, transgressed by the wicked, since this is against the law natural and written, divine and civil. It can also be referred to the destruction of the law of Moses, which the Chaldeans tore in pieces by burning the library of the Jews, which Esdras afterwards restored. [[1:4|and judgment cometh not to the end|Et non pervenit usque ad finem judicium]], that is, it has not had a just outcome. For the end of judgment is that each one receive what he has deserved, the good honour, the wicked punishment; but because of what has been said the opposite has come about, as far as the present life is concerned. [[1:4|because the wicked prevaileth against the just|Quia impius praevalet adversus justum]], namely the king and army of Babylon against the Jewish people, among whom certain just men were carried away and taken captive, such as Daniel, Azarias, Ananias and Misael, and Ezechiel; [[1:4|therefore wrong judgment goeth forth|propterea egreditur judicium perversum]], not from God, but from the Chaldeans against the Jews, whom they often cruelly oppressed.

paras.t: Hucusque conquestus est Propheta populi sui persecutionem : cujus dolorem mitigat Dominus, eo quod ceterae gentes similia sint passurae. Adspicite, o Judaei, in gentibus, quae fient in eis, et videte, et admiramini, et obstupescite propter magnitudinem rei quam dico, quia opus factum est in diebus vestris, id est, statim fiet, jamque partim factum est seu inceptum, quod nemo credet, quum narrabitur, id est, non faciliter credetur ab his qui illud non conspexerunt.
paras.en: Thus far the Prophet has complained of the persecution of his people; and the Lord softens his grief by this, that the other nations are to suffer the like. [[1:5|Behold ye|Adspicite]], O Jews, [[1:5|among the nations|in gentibus]] what shall be done among them, [[1:5|and see|et videte]], [[1:5|wonder, and be astonished|et admiramini, et obstupescite]] at the greatness of the thing I speak of, [[1:5|for a work is done in your days|quia opus factum est in diebus vestris]], that is, it will be done at once, and is already in part done or begun, [[1:5|which no man will believe when it shall be told|quod nemo credet, quum narrabitur]], that is, it will not easily be believed by those who have not seen it.

paras.t: Quid autem sit opus istud tam mirum, subjungitur : Quia ecce ego Deus, qui peccata unius gentis per aliam vindico, suscitabo, dando virtutem et inspirando affectum, Chaldaeos, gentem amaram, id est crudelem, et velocem, ambulantem super latitudinem terrae, id est suis finibus non contentam, sed huc illucque vagantem, et loca non sua occupantem : ideo subditur, ut possideat tabernacula non sua. Hoc tamen referri potest ad id quod Dominus dixit, Suscitabo. Ad hoc namque Dominus induxit Chaldaeos ad impugnandum gentium regna, ut eadem possiderent quasi pro mercede, quia divinae voluntati servierunt in expugnatione punitioneque gentium. Unde ad Ezechielem testatur, se daturum Chaldaeis terram et bona Aegypti, pro servitio quod sibi in expugnatione Tyri impenderunt. Sic ergo possederunt tabernacula quae ante non erant sua, sed Deo ea illis donante, erant sua. Verumtamen, quia non ea intentione ista fecerunt, qua Deus eos suscitavit, sed ex cupiditate, crudelitate, et elatione, abusique sunt potestate sibi collata, idcirco non excusantur a culpa, imo a Medis ac Persis meruerunt vastari.
paras.en: What this so wonderful work is, is added: [[1:6|For behold|Quia ecce]] I, God, who avenge the sins of one nation by means of another, [[1:6|I will raise up|suscitabo]], by giving them strength and inspiring the will, [[1:6|the Chaldeans, a bitter|Chaldaeos, gentem amaram]] nation, that is, a cruel one, [[1:6|and swift|et velocem]], [[1:6|marching upon the breadth of the earth|ambulantem super latitudinem terrae]], that is, not content with its own borders, but roving hither and thither and seizing places not its own: and so it is added, [[1:6|to possess the dwelling places that are not their own|ut possideat tabernacula non sua]]. This, however, can be referred to what the Lord said, [[1:6|I will raise up|Suscitabo]]. For the Lord led the Chaldeans to attack the kingdoms of the nations to this end, that they might possess them as it were for wages, because they served the divine will in conquering and punishing the nations. Hence he testifies to Ezechiel that he would give the Chaldeans the land and goods of Egypt[[Ezech 29:19||]][[Ezech 29:20||]] for the service they had done him in the siege of Tyre. So they possessed dwellings that before were not their own, but, God giving them to them, were their own. Yet, because they did not do these things with the intention with which God raised them up, but out of greed, cruelty and pride, and abused the power granted them, they are therefore not excused from guilt; nay, they deserved to be laid waste by the Medes and Persians.

paras.t: Horribilis et terribilis est, id est, fama et re, adspectu et opere metuendi sunt. Erant enim Chaldaei, secundum historiographos, bellicosissimi, veloces, nimiumque feroces. Ex semetipsa judicium ejus et onus ejus egredietur, id est, ex propria voluntate tyrannica, non ex censura justitiae procedet judicium ejus et persecutio, quibus alios judicabit et persequetur. Vel sensus est, quod ex actibus suis crudelibus merebitur judicari atque puniri a Deo, ut sicut fecit, fiat ei, et vastetur sicut vastavit. Aut certe iste est sensus, quod ex propria gente constituet judices et punitores saevissimos.
paras.en: [[1:7|They are dreadful, and terrible|Horribilis et terribilis est]], that is, they are to be feared in report and in fact, in look and in deed. For the Chaldeans, according to the historians, were most warlike, swift, and exceedingly fierce. [[1:7|from themselves shall their judgment, and their burden proceed|Ex semetipsa judicium ejus et onus ejus egredietur]] [the Latin speaks of the nation in the singular: "from itself shall its judgment and its burden proceed"], that is, from its own tyrannical will, not from the sentence of justice, shall proceed its judgment and persecution, by which it will judge and persecute others. Or the sense is that by its own cruel deeds it will deserve to be judged and punished by God, so that as it has done, so it may be done to it, and it may be laid waste as it has laid waste. Or else this is the sense, that it will appoint judges and most savage punishers from its own nation.

paras.t: Leviores pardis equi ejus, et velociores lupis vespertinis. Per hoc, quantum ad comparationem pardorum, hyperbolice insinuatur magna valde velocitas equorum populi hujus. Pardus autem est animal velocissimum, pulchra varietate distinctum. De quo Jeremias : Si mutare, inquit, potest pardus varietates suas. Praeterea lupi vespertini saeviores sunt diurna fame irritati : unde circa vesperam velocius currunt, escam praedamque petentes. Et diffundentur equites ejus, id est, equestres gentis Chaldaeae terram operient sicut locustae.
paras.en: [[1:8|Their horses are lighter than leopards|Leviores pardis equi ejus]], [[1:8|and swifter than evening wolves|et velociores lupis vespertinis]]. By this, as regards the comparison with leopards, a very great swiftness of the horses of this people is suggested by hyperbole. Now the leopard is a very swift animal, marked with a beautiful variety of colours. Of it Jeremias says: If, he says, [[Jer 13:23|the leopard|pardus]] can change [[Jer 13:23|his spots|varietates suas]]. Moreover evening wolves are fiercer, being stirred up by the hunger of the day: hence towards evening they run more swiftly, seeking food and prey. [[1:8|and their horsemen shall be spread abroad|Et diffundentur equites ejus]], that is, the horsemen of the Chaldean nation shall cover the earth like locusts.

paras.t: Equites namque ejus de longe venient, id est a Chaldæa usque ad loca inde remota, volabunt quasi aquila festinans ad comedendum. Omnes ad prædam venient, id est, ultra modum velociter invadent gentes et regna, quemadmodum aquila famelica properat ad cadaver. Facies eorum ventus urens: id est, quemadmodum talis ventus faciem lædit, segetesque corrumpit, sic Chaldæi ipso adspectu affligent intuentes, et cuncta vastabunt.
paras.en: [[1:8|for their horsemen shall come from afar|Equites namque ejus de longe venient]], that is, from Chaldea even to places far removed from it; [[1:8|they shall fly as an eagle that maketh haste to eat|volabunt quasi aquila festinans ad comedendum]]. [[1:9|They shall all come to the prey|Omnes ad prædam venient]], that is, they will fall upon nations and kingdoms with exceeding swiftness, as a famished eagle hastens to a carcass. [[1:9|their face is like a burning wind|Facies eorum ventus urens]]: that is, as such a wind hurts the face and spoils the crops, so the Chaldeans will afflict those who behold them by their very look, and will lay all things waste.

paras.t: Et congregabit rex atque exercitus Chaldæorum, quasi arenam captivitatem, id est, innumerabiles capiet in diversis provinciis. Et ipse de regibus triumphabit: nullus enim regum resistere potuit Nabuchodonosor. Propter quod Daniel dixit ad eum : Tu rex regum es. Et tyranni ridiculi ejus erunt, id est derisionis materia, ita quod derisui eos habebit, faciliter vincet, raptosque ante se currere faciet: quod inter delicias suas computabit, quum sit signum potentiæ suæ. Ipse super omnem munitionem ridebit, id est, certam sibi victoriam de quacumque munitione promittet, reputans se urbes armatura et viribus hominum roboratas faciliter devicturum; et comportabit aggerem, implendo loca profunda lignis et saxis, ut possint transire. Hoc maxime fecit ante Tyrum in mari sitam. Et capiet eam, id est quamlibet munitionem a se impugnatam.
paras.en: [[1:9|and they shall gather together|Et congregabit]], namely the king and army of the Chaldeans, [[1:9|captives as the sand|quasi arenam captivitatem]], that is, he will take numberless captives in divers provinces. [[1:10|And their prince shall triumph over kings|Et ipse de regibus triumphabit]]: for none of the kings could withstand Nabuchodonosor. Wherefore Daniel said to him: [[Dan 2:37|Thou art a king of kings|Tu rex regum es]][[Dan 4:19||]]. [[1:10|and princes shall be his laughingstock|Et tyranni ridiculi ejus erunt]], that is, matter for derision, so that he will hold them in derision, conquer them easily, and make them run captive before him: which he will count among his delights, since it is a sign of his power. [[1:10|and he shall laugh at every strong hold|Ipse super omnem munitionem ridebit]], that is, he will promise himself sure victory over any stronghold whatever, reckoning that he will easily overcome cities strengthened with arms and the might of men; [[1:10|and shall cast up a mount|et comportabit aggerem]], filling deep places with timber and stones so that they could cross. This he did above all before Tyre, which stands in the sea. [[1:10|and shall take it|Et capiet eam]], that is, any stronghold he attacks.

paras.t: Tunc mutabitur spiritus ejus, id est, post tantas victorias in maximam superbiam erigetur. Vel mutabitur spiritus ejus, id est, amens fiet ac insensatus. Usu enim rationis amisso, putabit se bestiam, et inter feras conversans, fœnum comedet ut bos, juxta illud in Daniele : Ex hominibus ejicient te, et cum feris erit habitatio tua. Et pertransibit, id est, a statu et gloria regiæ sublimitatis deficiet, secundum quod dicitur apud Danielem : Tibi dicitur, Nabuchodonosor, Regnum transiit a te; et corruet, id est, post hæc se humiliabit, mortalem cognoscet, et esse desistet. Hæc est fortitudo ejus, dei sui, id est, talis fuit fortitudo regis istius, qualis et Belis dei sui. Fortitudo enim Nabuchodonosor fragilis fuit et labilis, quemadmodum idoli sui quod coluit nomine Bel.
paras.en: [[1:11|Then shall his spirit be changed|Tunc mutabitur spiritus ejus]], that is, after such great victories he will be lifted up into the greatest pride. Or, [[1:11|his spirit be changed|mutabitur spiritus ejus]], that is, he will become mad and senseless. For, having lost the use of reason, he will think himself a beast, and living among the wild beasts he will eat grass like an ox, according to that in Daniel: [[Dan 4:29|And they shall cast thee out from among men|Ex hominibus ejicient te]], [[Dan 4:29|and thy dwelling shall be with cattle and wild beasts|et cum feris erit habitatio tua]]. [[1:11|and he shall pass|Et pertransibit]], that is, he will fall away from the state and glory of royal majesty, according to what is said in Daniel: [[Dan 4:28|To thee, O king Nabuchodonosor, it is said: Thy kingdom shall pass from thee|Tibi dicitur, Nabuchodonosor, Regnum transiit a te]] [Denis reads *transiit*, "hath passed"]; [[1:11|and fall|et corruet]], that is, after this he will humble himself, acknowledge himself mortal, and cease to be. [[1:11|this is his strength of his god|Hæc est fortitudo ejus, dei sui]], that is, the strength of this king was such as was that of Bel his god. For the strength of Nabuchodonosor was frail and slippery, like that of his idol, which he worshipped under the name of Bel.

paras.t: Præterea veritati divinæ naturæ congratulans, divinæ quoque æquitati applaudens, Propheta annectit : Numquid non tu a principio? id est, imo tu solus æternus es, Domine Deus meus : qui licet sis omnium Deus generali providentia et jure creationis, specialiter tamen es Deus meus et electorum, tam ex parte tui, qui singulariter benefacis ac provides nobis, quam ex parte nostri, qui te summe diligimus, totaque mente tibi inhæremus; sancte meus, id est sanctificator animæ meæ, qui essentialiter sanctus es, et quem tanquam incomparabiliter sanctum in sanctitate colo; et non moriemur, id est, tua nos protegente clementia, non penitus a Chaldæis occidemur, sed temporaliter corrigemur.
paras.en: Further, rejoicing in the truth of the divine nature, and applauding the divine equity as well, the Prophet adds: [[1:12|Wast thou not from the beginning|Numquid non tu a principio]]? that is, nay, thou alone art eternal, [[1:12|O Lord my God|Domine Deus meus]]: who, though thou art the God of all by general providence and by right of creation, art yet in a special way my God and the God of the elect, as well on thy part, who in a singular manner dost good to us and providest for us, as on ours, who love thee above all things and cleave to thee with our whole mind; [[1:12|my holy one|sancte meus]], that is, the sanctifier of my soul, who art holy by thy essence, and whom, as incomparably holy, I worship in holiness; [[1:12|and we shall not die|et non moriemur]], that is, with thy clemency protecting us we shall not be utterly slain by the Chaldeans, but shall be corrected for a time.

paras.t: Consequenter Propheta ostendit se divinitus illustratum, et aperit causam superioris quæstionis et querelæ quam movit, cur scilicet Deus taceret, conculcante impio justiorem se. Domine, in judicium posuisti eum : id est, Nabuchodonosor in solio regali et tanta eminentia constituisti, ut per eum tuæ justitiæ judicium exsequereris; et fortem, ut corriperes, fundasti eum: id est, regem istum in tanta potestate fundasti seu fortem statuisti, ut per ejus potentiam corriperes gentes iniquas, earum peccata ulciscendo, et ipsas in manum Chaldæorum tradendo.
paras.en: Next, the Prophet shows that he has been enlightened by God, and discloses the reason for the question and complaint he raised above, namely why God held his peace while the wicked trod down the man more just than himself. [[1:12|Lord, thou hast appointed him for judgment|Domine, in judicium posuisti eum]]: that is, thou hast set Nabuchodonosor on the royal throne and in such great eminence, that through him thou mightest carry out the judgment of thy justice; [[1:12|and made him strong for correction|et fortem, ut corriperes, fundasti eum]] [literally "and thou hast founded him strong, that thou mightest correct"]: that is, thou hast founded this king in such great power, or established him strong, that by his might thou mightest chastise wicked nations, avenging their sins and delivering them into the hand of the Chaldeans.

paras.t: Mundi sunt oculi tui, ne videas malum, et respicere ad iniquitatem non poteris. Hoc dupliciter legi potest : Primo, inquirendo et abnegando, vel in persona imperfectorum, quia sic esse videtur; eritque sensus : Quum sis totaliter sanctus, non vis attendere vel adspicere vitia hominum : quod apparet per hoc, quod non statim adhibes ultionem. Secundo sic : Mundi sunt oculi tui, id est, intellectus tuus et sapientia absque omni sunt culpa, ne videas malum culpæ per approbationem, et respicere ad iniquitatem non poteris, ea (ut dictum est) approbando. Unde et impiis dicit : Nescio vos.
paras.en: [[1:13|Thy eyes are too pure to behold evil, and thou canst not look on iniquity|Mundi sunt oculi tui, ne videas malum, et respicere ad iniquitatem non poteris]] [literally "Thy eyes are clean, that thou see not evil, and thou canst not look upon iniquity"]. This can be read in two ways. First, by way of inquiry and denial [that is, as a question expecting the answer no], or in the person of the imperfect, because it seems so; and the sense will be: since thou art wholly holy, thou wilt not attend to or look upon the vices of men; which appears from this, that thou dost not straightway apply vengeance. Secondly thus: [[1:13|Thy eyes are too pure|Mundi sunt oculi tui]], that is, thy understanding and wisdom are without any fault, [[1:13|to behold evil|ne videas malum]], the evil of guilt, by approving it, [[1:13|and thou canst not look on iniquity|et respicere ad iniquitatem non poteris]] by approving it, as has been said. Hence he also says to the wicked: [[Matt 25:12|I know you not|Nescio vos]].

paras.t: Quum ergo sit ita, Quare non respicis per vindictam super inique agentes, et taces devorante impio justiorem se? Et facies homines quasi pisces maris, et quasi reptile non habens principem. Istud totum jam semel habitum est atque expositum. Sed mirum videtur, cur Propheta quæstionem hanc repetit, quum jam semel solverit eam. Et respondendum, quod quæstio ista generaliter accipi potest, non de Chaldæis dumtaxat; vel propter novam admirationem animo Prophetæ incidentem, repetit eam, loquens in persona impatientium hominum, vel justorum rationem divini judicii comprehendere non potentium.
paras.en: Since, then, it is so, [[1:13|Why lookest thou|Quare non respicis]] not, by way of vengeance, [[1:13|upon them that do unjust things|super inique agentes]], [[1:13|and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself?|et taces devorante impio justiorem se?]] [[1:14|And thou wilt make men as the fishes of the sea, and as the creeping things that have no ruler.|Et facies homines quasi pisces maris, et quasi reptile non habens principem.]] All this has already been had once and expounded[[1:3||]] [the margin refers to v. 3, at which Denis treated these words above]. But it seems strange that the Prophet should repeat this question, since he has already solved it once. And the answer must be that this question can be taken generally, not of the Chaldeans only; or else he repeats it because of a fresh wonder that has come upon the Prophet's mind, speaking in the person of impatient men, or of just men who cannot grasp the reason of the divine judgment.

paras.t: Totum in hamo sublevavit : id est, sicut piscator per hamum capit et elevat pisces, sic Nabuchodonosor sua virtute in calliditate cepit quos voluit; traxit illud in sagena sua, id est, lata sua potestate subjecit captivos, ita quod fugere seu evadere non valebant, et congregavit in rete suum, id est, suo imperio atque carceribus illos inclusit. Super hoc, id est de tantis prædis hominum atque triumphis, lætabitur corde, et exsultabit corpore, signa interioris lætitiæ demonstrando.
paras.en: [[1:15|He lifted up all them with his hook|Totum in hamo sublevavit]]: that is, as a fisherman takes and lifts up fish by a hook, so Nabuchodonosor by his power, with cunning, took whom he would; [[1:15|he drew them in his drag|traxit illud in sagena sua]] [*sagena*, a dragnet], that is, by his wide-reaching power he subjected the captives, so that they could not flee or escape, [[1:15|and gathered them into his net|et congregavit in rete suum]], that is, shut them up in his empire and his prisons. [[1:15|for this|Super hoc]], that is, over such great spoils of men and such triumphs, [[1:15|he will be glad|lætabitur]] in heart, [[1:15|and rejoice|et exsultabit]] in body, showing signs of the gladness within.

paras.t: Propterea immolabit sagenæ suæ, et sacrificabit reti suo : id est, ob istas victorias offeret victimas magnas deo seu idolo suo, cujus virtute atque auxilio putavit se prævaluisse : ideo nomine sagenæ ac retis exprimitur. Quia in ipsis incrassata est pars ejus, et cibus ejus electus : id est, imperium ejus ditatum est per direptionem ac spoliationem factam per sagenam et rete superius dicta, vel virtute idolorum suorum, secundum suam opinionem.
paras.en: [[1:16|Therefore will he offer victims to his drag|Propterea immolabit sagenæ suæ]], [[1:16|and he will sacrifice to his net|et sacrificabit reti suo]]: that is, for these victories he will offer great victims to his god or idol, by whose power and help he thought he had prevailed: and so it is expressed under the name of drag and net. [[1:16|because through them his portion is made fat, and his meat dainty|Quia in ipsis incrassata est pars ejus, et cibus ejus electus]]: that is, his empire has been enriched by the pillage and spoiling done by the drag and net spoken of above, or by the power of his idols, according to his opinion.

paras.t: Propter hoc ergo expandit sagenam suam, id est potestatem atque exercitum suum super terram et gentes; et semper interficere gentes non cessat, id est, indesinenter horis solitis, quoadusque durat ejus crudelitas, interimit gentes, nunc unam, nunc aliam, nec sanguine satiatur humano.
paras.en: [[1:17|For this cause therefore he spreadeth his net|Propter hoc ergo expandit sagenam suam]], that is, his power and his army, over the earth and the nations; [[1:17|and will not spare continually to slay the nations|et semper interficere gentes non cessat]] [Denis reads *non cessat*, "ceaseth not", where the Vulgate has *non parcet*, "will not spare"], that is, unceasingly, at the accustomed hours, so long as his cruelty lasts, he slays the nations, now one, now another, and is not sated with human blood.

1.title: Expositio tropologica.
1.title_en: Tropological exposition [that is, the moral reading] of the same first chapter.

paras.t: Denique Habacuc interpretatur amplexans, vel amplexatio. Qui ergo spiritualiter Habacuc est, Deum brachiis caritatis stringendo, aut per modum pie luctantis amplexando, donec benedicatur, illuminetur et exaudiatur ab ipso, hic conspicit Onus Babylonis, id est mundi hujus miseriam, præsentisque vitæ fragilitatem, et futuræ damnationis intolerabile pondus, sæculi amatoribus præparatum.
paras.en: Lastly, Habacuc is interpreted "embracing" or "embrace". He therefore who is spiritually a Habacuc, holding God fast in the arms of charity, or embracing Him after the manner of one who wrestles in devotion, until he is blessed, enlightened and heard by Him, beholds [[1:1|The burden|Onus]] of Babylon, that is, the misery of this world, the frailty of the present life, and the unbearable weight of the damnation to come, made ready for the lovers of the world.

paras.t: Talis insuper Dei fervidus amplexator, et familiaris cum eo disputator, pro sua ac aliorum ereptione et consolatione instanter orans, nec tamen ad votum exaudiri se videns, piam agat querelam, ut clementiam provocet Creatoris, dicatque : Usquequo, Domine, clamabo, et non exaudies? qui tamen dixisti : Omnis qui petit, accipit; et qui quærit, invenit. Et rursus : Si quid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, hoc faciam. Vociferabor ad te, vim patiens, id est validam impugnationem a propriis passionibus, a mundo persequente aut adulante, et item ab invisibilibus hostibus, et non salvabis me ab istis molestiis? quum tamen promiseris, Omnis quicumque invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit. Porro tanto altius vociferamur, quanto affectuosius deprecamur, etiam si nullam vocem formemus : quia non tam clamor oris, quam amor cordis sonat in auribus Dei. Hoc affectu videtur Psalmista locutus, dicendo : Usquequo, Domine, oblivisceris me in finem ? usquequo avertis faciem tuam a me? Quamdiu ponam consilia in anima mea? Usquequo exaltabitur inimicus meus super me? Et sanctus Job : Clamo ad te, et non exaudis me; sto, et non respicis me; mutatus es mihi in crudelem. Verum in hac dilatione, quantumcumque morosa, servanda est patientia inconcussa, atque fiducia in Deo certissima, ut in omni angustia certissimi simus impossibile esse sperantem in Domino derelinqui, aut indesinenter orantem repelli, et Deum propter profectum nostrum differre precis nostræ effectum, aut aliud salubrius se esse daturum.
paras.en: Moreover, such a fervent embracer of God, who speaks with Him familiarly, praying earnestly for his own deliverance and consolation and that of others, and yet not seeing himself heard as he wishes, may make a devout complaint, to move the clemency of the Creator, and say: [[1:2|How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear?|Usquequo, Domine, clamabo, et non exaudies]] Thou who hast said nevertheless: [[Luke 11:10|every one that asketh receiveth: and he that seeketh findeth|Omnis qui petit, accipit; et qui quærit, invenit]]. And again: [[John 14:14|If you shall ask|Si quid petieritis]] [[John 14:13|the Father in my name, that will I do|Patrem in nomine meo, hoc faciam]]. [[1:2|shall I cry out to thee suffering violence|Vociferabor ad te, vim patiens]], that is, a strong assault from my own passions, from the world persecuting or flattering me, and likewise from invisible enemies, [[1:2|and thou wilt not save|et non salvabis]] me from these troubles? And yet thou hast promised: [[Joel 2:32|every one that shall call upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved|Omnis quicumque invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit]]. Now, we cry out the louder the more lovingly we pray, even if we form no sound at all: for it is not so much the cry of the mouth as the love of the heart that sounds in the ears of God. With this affection the Psalmist seems to have spoken, saying: [[Ps 12:1|How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me unto the end? how long dost thou turn away thy face from me?|Usquequo, Domine, oblivisceris me in finem ? usquequo avertis faciem tuam a me?]] [[Ps 12:2|How long shall I take counsels in my soul|Quamdiu ponam consilia in anima mea]]? [[Ps 12:3|How long shall my enemy be exalted over me|Usquequo exaltabitur inimicus meus super me]]? And holy Job: [[Job 30:20|I cry to thee, and thou hearest me not: I stand up, and thou dost not regard me|Clamo ad te, et non exaudis me; sto, et non respicis me]]; [[Job 30:21|Thou art changed to be cruel toward me|mutatus es mihi in crudelem]]. But in this delay, however long it lasts, patience must be kept unshaken and a most certain trust in God, so that in every distress we may be entirely certain that it is impossible for one who hopes in the Lord to be forsaken, or for one who prays without ceasing to be rejected; and that God, for our progress, puts off the granting of our prayer, or else will give something else more wholesome.

paras.t: Præterea talis Dei amplexator, considerans Ecclesiam a suis æmulis multipliciter tribulari, bonos a pravis affligi, electos a reprobis opprimi, ex compassione ingenti dicere potest in persona sua atque Ecclesiæ : Quare ostendisti mihi iniquitatem, et laborem videre, id est malitiam impiorum adversus electos, et electorum fatigationem sive laborem quem eis infligunt perversi, prædam et injustitiam contra me? Hostes etenim animarum, interiora gratiæ bona et exteriora bona nituntur justis auferre. Hoc affectu dixit venerabilis ille Mathathias, Judæorum gravissima persecutione perspecta : Heu! cur natus sum videre mala gentis meæ? Sed ista querela debet esse moderata, ut non ignoremus dispensationem divini judicii, quo boni in hoc sæculo adversis purgantur, mali vero periculosissime prosperantur. Hinc nempe dixit Psalmista : Noli æmulari in malignantibus, neque zelaveris facientes iniquitatem, quoniam tanquam fœnum velociter arescent. Et Christus : Si me persecuti sunt, et vos persequentur, quia non est servus major domino suo. Paulus quoque : Nemo, inquit, moveatur in tribulationibus istis.
paras.en: Further, such an embracer of God, seeing the Church troubled in many ways by her rivals, the good afflicted by the wicked, the elect oppressed by the reprobate, can say out of great compassion, in his own person and in that of the Church: [[1:3|Why hast thou shewn me iniquity and grievance, to see|Quare ostendisti mihi iniquitatem, et laborem videre]] [*laborem*, "toil", which the Douay-Rheims renders "grievance"], that is, the malice of the wicked against the elect, and the weariness or toil of the elect which the perverse inflict on them, [[1:3|rapine and injustice before me|prædam et injustitiam contra me]]? For the enemies of souls strive to take from the just both the inward goods of grace and their outward goods. In this affection that venerable Mathathias spoke, when he saw the most grievous persecution of the Jews: [[1 Mach 2:7|Woe is me, wherefore was I born to see|Heu! cur natus sum videre]] [[1 Mach 3:59|the evils of our nation|mala gentis meæ]]? [the second half is from the words of Judas Machabeus at 1 Mach 3:59, as the margin also notes] But this complaint ought to be moderate, so that we are not ignorant of the dispensation of the divine judgment, by which the good are purged by adversity in this world, while the wicked prosper, to their very great peril. Hence indeed the Psalmist said: [[Ps 36:1|Be not emulous of evildoers; nor envy them that work iniquity|Noli æmulari in malignantibus, neque zelaveris facientes iniquitatem]]; [[Ps 36:2|For they shall shortly wither away as grass|quoniam tanquam fœnum velociter arescent]]. And Christ: [[John 15:20|If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you|Si me persecuti sunt, et vos persequentur]], for the [[John 15:20|servant is not greater than his master|non est servus major domino suo]]. And Paul: [[1 Thess 3:3|no man|Nemo]], he says, [[1 Thess 3:3|should be moved in these tribulations|moveatur in tribulationibus istis]].

paras.t: Quare respicis contemptores, id est divinæ legis transgressores, superbos, inobedientes, rebelles, dando eis bona vitæ præsentis, honorem, gloriam, famam, prolem, divitias? De quibus fertur in Psalmo : Ecce ipsi peccatores et abundantes in sæculo, obtinuerunt divitias. His ergo benignus est Deus, et in hoc ejus bonitatem imitari debemus, quemadmodum ait Salvator : Eritis filii Altissimi, quia ipse benignus est super ingratos et malos ; et alibi : Diligite inimicos vestros, et benefacite his qui oderunt vos, ut sitis filii Patris vestri qui in cœlis est, qui solem suum facit oriri super bonos ac malos, et pluit super justos et injustos. Et taces, conculcante impio justiorem se? Quomodo verba hæc exponi possint in persona perfectorum et imperfectorum, dictum est in præcedenti articulo. Si autem in persona imperfectorum exponantur, competunt his de quibus apud Malachiam loquitur Dominus : Invaluerunt super me verba vestra, et dixistis : Vanus est qui servit Domino; et quod emolumentum, quia ambulavimus tristes coram Domino? Ergo nunc beatos dicimus arrogantes, siquidem ædificati sunt.
paras.en: [[1:13|Why lookest thou|Quare respicis]] upon the despisers [Denis's text of the prophet, here as in the previous article, has these words, *Quare respicis contemptores, et taces conculcante impio justiorem se? Et facies homines quasi pisces maris*, in the course of v. 3; in the Douay-Rheims they answer to vv. 13–14], that is, the transgressors of the divine law, the proud, the disobedient, the rebellious, giving them the goods of the present life, honour, glory, fame, offspring, riches? Of whom it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 72:12|Behold these are sinners; and yet, abounding in the world they have obtained riches|Ecce ipsi peccatores et abundantes in sæculo, obtinuerunt divitias]]. To these, then, God is kind, and in this we ought to imitate His goodness, as the Saviour says: [[Luke 6:35|you shall be the sons of the Highest. For he is kind to the unthankful and to the evil|Eritis filii Altissimi, quia ipse benignus est super ingratos et malos]]; and elsewhere: [[Matt 5:44|Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you|Diligite inimicos vestros, et benefacite his qui oderunt vos]], [[Matt 5:45|That you may be the children of your Father who is in heaven, who maketh his sun to rise upon the good, and bad, and raineth upon the just and the unjust|ut sitis filii Patris vestri qui in cœlis est, qui solem suum facit oriri super bonos ac malos, et pluit super justos et injustos]]. [[1:13|and holdest thy peace|Et taces]], while the wicked man treadeth down [[1:13|the man that is more just than himself|justiorem se]]? How these words can be expounded in the person of the perfect and of the imperfect was said in the previous article. But if they are expounded in the person of the imperfect, they fit those of whom the Lord speaks in Malachias: [[Mal 3:13|Your words have been unsufferable to me|Invaluerunt super me verba vestra]], [[Mal 3:14|And you have said|et dixistis]]: [[Mal 3:14|He laboureth in vain that serveth God, and what profit is it|Vanus est qui servit Domino; et quod emolumentum]], [[Mal 3:14|that we have walked sorrowful before the Lord|quia ambulavimus tristes coram Domino]]? [[Mal 3:15|Wherefore now we call the proud people happy|Ergo nunc beatos dicimus arrogantes]], since they [[Mal 3:15|are built up|siquidem ædificati sunt]].

paras.t: Et facies homines quasi pisces maris. Si hoc juxta sensum præinductum asserendo dicatur, competit negantibus providentiam Dei. De quibus habetur in Psalmo : Et dixerunt, Quomodo scit Deus, et si est scientia in Excelso? In Job quoque : An cogitas quod Deus excelsior cœlo sit, nec nostra considerat, et circa cardines cœli perambulat? Hic error tribuit securitatem peccandi.
paras.en: [[1:14|And thou wilt make men as the fishes of the sea|Et facies homines quasi pisces maris]]. If this is said as an assertion, in the sense set out before, it fits those who deny the providence of God. Of whom we have in the Psalm: [[Ps 72:11|And they said: How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?|Et dixerunt, Quomodo scit Deus, et si est scientia in Excelso?]] And in Job too: [[Job 22:12|Dost not thou think that God is higher than heaven|An cogitas quod Deus excelsior cœlo sit]], and that [[Job 22:14|he doth not consider our things, and he walketh about the poles of heaven|nec nostra considerat, et circa cardines cœli perambulat?]]? This error gives a false security in sinning.

paras.t: Et factum est judicium perversum, dum judices intuitu munerum, vel favore, timore, aut odio damnant insontem, et liberant reum. Quibus ait Psalmista : Usquequo judicatis iniquitatem, et facies peccatorum sumitis? Propter hoc lacerata est lex, id est, præcepta evangelicæ doctrinæ non custodiuntur a judicibus et prælatis ambitiosis ac cupidis : et ex consequenti, neque a subditis, quia secundum judicem populi, sic et ministri ejus. Unde necesse habemus orare : Tempus faciendi, Domine, videlicet quod postulo, dissipaverunt legem tuam.
paras.en: [[1:3|and there is a judgment|Et factum est judicium]], a perverse one [Denis's lemma joins "there is a judgment" of v. 3 to the "wrong (*perversum*) judgment" of v. 4], when judges, with an eye to gifts, or out of favour, fear or hatred, condemn the innocent and set free the guilty. To whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 81:2|How long will you judge unjustly: and accept the persons of the wicked?|Usquequo judicatis iniquitatem, et facies peccatorum sumitis?]] [[1:4|Therefore the law is torn in pieces|Propter hoc lacerata est lex]], that is, the precepts of the gospel teaching are not kept by ambitious and covetous judges and prelates, and in consequence not by their subjects either, since: [[Ecclus 10:2|As the judge of the people is himself, so also are his ministers|secundum judicem populi, sic et ministri ejus]]. Hence we must needs pray: [[Ps 118:126|It is time, O Lord, to do|Tempus faciendi, Domine]], namely, what I ask: [[Ps 118:126|they have dissipated thy law|dissipaverunt legem tuam]].

paras.t: Ecce ego suscitabo Chaldæos, gentem amaram et velocem. Per Chaldæos figurantur diaboli, secundum quod Christus de dæmone ait in Evangelio, Inimicus homo hoc fecit: qui suscitantur a Deo, dum præstat eis licentiam tentandi tribulandique homines, quemadmodum fertur de quibusdam in Psalmo: Misit in eos iram indignationis suæ, immissiones per angelos malos. Ambulantem super latitudinem terræ: secundum quod Satan ait ad Dominum, Circuivi terram, et perambulavi eam. Vel latitudo terræ, sunt corda carnalium, lata via tendentium ad infernum. Ut possideat tabernacula non sua, id est homines impœnitentes, quos Deus dat in reprobum sensum: qui sunt Dei ex conditione, sed per iniquitatem efficiuntur tabernacula dæmonum, qui ingressi habitant ibi. Unde de diabolo loquitur Christus: Quum fortis armatus custodit atrium suum, in pace sunt ea quæ possidet. Horribilis et terribilis est. Quid enim callidius aut crudelius seu pœnalius dæmone? quid invidiosius aut nocentius eo? Propter quod admonet Petrus: Sobrii estote et vigilate, quia adversarius vester diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret. Ex semetipsa judicium ejus, id est, propria elatione meruit condemnari: quod maxime competit primo apostatæ angelo, qui nullius suggestione, sed propriæ adinventionis superbia est damnatus. Alii vero ejus suggestione peccaverunt.
paras.en: [[1:6|behold, I will raise up the Chaldeans, a bitter and swift nation|Ecce ego suscitabo Chaldæos, gentem amaram et velocem]]. By the Chaldeans the devils are figured, as Christ says of the demon in the Gospel: [[Matt 13:28|An enemy hath done this|Inimicus homo hoc fecit]]. They are raised up by God when He grants them leave to tempt and trouble men, as is said of some in the Psalm: [[Ps 77:49|he sent upon them the wrath of his indignation|Misit in eos iram indignationis suæ]], [[Ps 77:49|which he sent by evil angels|immissiones per angelos malos]]. [[1:6|marching upon the breadth of the earth|Ambulantem super latitudinem terræ]]: as Satan says to the Lord: [[Job 1:7|I have gone round about the earth, and walked through it|Circuivi terram, et perambulavi eam]]. Or the breadth of the earth is the hearts of carnal men, who go by the broad way to hell. [[1:6|to possess the dwelling places that are not their own|Ut possideat tabernacula non sua]], that is, impenitent men, whom God gives up to a reprobate sense: they are God's by their creation, but through iniquity they are made the tabernacles of the demons, who enter in and dwell there. Hence Christ says of the devil: [[Luke 11:21|When a strong man armed keepeth his court, those things are in peace which he possesseth|Quum fortis armatus custodit atrium suum, in pace sunt ea quæ possidet]]. [[1:7|They are dreadful, and terrible|Horribilis et terribilis est]]. For what is more cunning, more cruel or more hurtful than the demon? What more envious or more harmful than he? Wherefore Peter warns: [[1 Pet 5:8|Be sober and watch: because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour|Sobrii estote et vigilate, quia adversarius vester diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret]]. [[1:7|from themselves shall their judgment|Ex semetipsa judicium ejus]], that is, by his own pride he deserved to be condemned: which fits above all the first apostate angel, who was damned at no one's suggestion but by the pride of his own devising. The others sinned at his suggestion.

paras.t: Leviores, id est ad peccata velociores, sunt pardis equi ejus, id est homines vitiosi, super quos equitat diabolus, ducens eos quocumque voluerit, juxta illud Apostoli: A quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem. Et diffundentur equites ejus, id est angeli Satanæ, qui in aere volitant, et ubique homines tentant: qui veniunt de longe, id est ab aere caliginoso sive inferno. Volabunt quasi aquila. Sunt enim promptissimi ex magna invidia ad impugnandum homines. Facies eorum ventus urens: quoniam flatu suo igne concupiscentiæ corda incendunt ac urunt, et semen verbi cœlestis infructuosum efficiunt, dicente Filio Dei: Venit diabolus, et tollit verbum de corde eorum, ne salvi fiant.
paras.en: [[1:8|lighter|Leviores]], that is, swifter to sin, [[1:8|than leopards|pardis]] are his [[1:8|horses|equi ejus]], that is, vicious men, on whom the devil rides, leading them wherever he will, according to that saying of the Apostle: [[2 Tim 2:26|by whom they are held captive at his will|A quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem]]. [[1:8|and their horsemen shall be spread abroad|Et diffundentur equites ejus]], that is, the angels of Satan, who fly about in the air and tempt men everywhere; who [[1:8|shall come from afar|veniunt de longe]], that is, from the dark air, or from hell. [[1:8|they shall fly as an eagle|Volabunt quasi aquila]]. For out of their great envy they are most ready to assail men. [[1:9|their face is like a burning wind|Facies eorum ventus urens]]: for with their breath they kindle and burn hearts with the fire of concupiscence, and make the seed of the heavenly word unfruitful, as the Son of God says: [[Luke 8:12|the devil cometh and taketh the word out of their heart|Venit diabolus, et tollit verbum de corde eorum]], [[Luke 8:12|lest|ne]] [[Luke 8:12|they should be saved|salvi fiant]].

paras.t: Et congregabit quasi arenam captivitatem: id est, innumerabiles animas vinculo peccatorum constringit, servituti peccati substernit, et suo infelici subdit dominio. Qui enim volunt divites fieri, incidunt in laqueum diaboli: similiter omnes superbi, luxuriosi, cæterisque mortalibus vitiis involuti. Tales autem, sunt multi quasi arena. Et ipse de regibus triumphabit. Divites namque, magnates et nobiles sæculi facilius vincit. Ipse super omnem munitionem ridebit: quia et claustra regulari institutione firmata, magna jam ex parte ad regulæ seu statutorum transgressionem vitamque induxit carnalem; et comportabit aggerem, id est, diversa tentationum instrumenta et occasiones peccandi assumet contra claustrales, et capiet eam, id est munitionem, seu congregationem claustralem pertrahet ad peccata. Tunc mutabitur spiritus ejus in superbiam et pessimam gloriationem, de talium ruina vehementer exsultans; et pertransibit et corruet, id est, peribit, atque a Christo damnabitur, qui visitabit super militiam cœli et principes terræ, congregabitque eos congregatione unius fasciis, et claudentur in carcere.
paras.en: [[1:9|and they shall gather together captives as the sand|Et congregabit quasi arenam captivitatem]]: that is, he binds innumerable souls with the chain of sins, lays them under the servitude of sin, and subjects them to his unhappy dominion. For [[1 Tim 6:9|they that will become rich fall|Qui enim volunt divites fieri, incidunt]] [[1 Tim 6:9|into the snare of the devil|in laqueum diaboli]]; and so likewise all the proud, the lustful, and those entangled in the other mortal vices. And such are many, as the sand. [[1:10|And their prince shall triumph over kings|Et ipse de regibus triumphabit]]. For he more easily overcomes the rich, the great and the nobles of the world. [[1:10|he shall laugh at every strong hold|Ipse super omnem munitionem ridebit]]: for even the cloisters, made strong by regular institution, he has now in great part led into transgression of the rule or statutes, and into a carnal life; [[1:10|and shall cast up a mount|et comportabit aggerem]], that is, he will take up against religious various instruments of temptation and occasions of sin, [[1:10|and shall take it|et capiet eam]], that is, the stronghold: he will draw the religious community into sin. [[1:11|Then shall his spirit be changed|Tunc mutabitur spiritus ejus]] into pride and most wicked boasting [these words stand in Denis's lemma but not in the verse], exulting exceedingly over the ruin of such men; [[1:11|and he shall pass, and fall|et pertransibit et corruet]], that is, he will perish and be condemned by Christ, who [[Is 24:21|shall visit upon the host of heaven|visitabit super militiam cœli]] and the princes of the earth, and will gather them [[Is 24:22|in the gathering of one bundle|congregatione unius fasciis]], and [[Is 24:22|they shall be shut up there in prison|claudentur in carcere]] [Denis does not name the passage, Isaias 24:21–22, and gives it freely].

paras.t: Domine, in judicium posuisti eum. Hoc accipi potest de diabolo vel quocumque persecutore justorum atque tyranno, per quos Deus judicium suum exsequitur, ulciscendo per eos peccata hominum in præsenti sive futuro.
paras.en: [[1:12|Lord, thou hast appointed him for judgment|Domine, in judicium posuisti eum]]. This can be taken of the devil, or of any persecutor of the just and any tyrant, through whom God carries out His judgment, avenging through them the sins of men in the present life or in the life to come.

paras.t: Quare non respicis super inique agentes? Hoc dicere possumus zelo caritatis et æquitatis, optantes a Deo ut flagellet iniquos in præsenti sæculo, ne gravius damnentur in posterum; vel ut hostes fidei ac boni communis tollat e medio terræ, et ne permittat impios temporaliter prosperari, ne prosperitas talis fiat eis occasio majoris culpæ graviorisque pœnæ. Unde orat vir sanctus: Non miserearis omnibus qui operantur iniquitatem.
paras.en: [[1:13|Why lookest thou|Quare non respicis]] not [[1:13|upon them that do unjust things|super inique agentes]]? [Denis's text reads *Quare non respicis*, "Why lookest thou not", that is, to punish] We can say this out of zeal for charity and equity, asking God to scourge the wicked in the present world, lest they be more grievously damned hereafter; or to take away the enemies of the faith and of the common good from the midst of the earth, and not to allow the wicked to prosper in temporal things, lest such prosperity become for them an occasion of greater guilt and heavier punishment. Hence the holy man prays: [[Ps 58:6|have no mercy on all them that work iniquity|Non miserearis omnibus qui operantur iniquitatem]].

paras.t: Totum in hamo suo sublevavit, id est, diabolus sua tentatione universam generationem malorum comprehendit: quam trahit in sagena sua, id est multiformi fallacia, et congregat in rete suum, id est in infernum seu impiissimam dominationem. Super hoc lætabitur, quia de hominum deceptione gloriatur.
paras.en: [[1:15|He lifted up all them with his hook|Totum in hamo suo sublevavit]], that is, the devil by his temptation lays hold of the whole generation of the wicked, which he draws [[1:15|in his drag|in sagena sua]] [that is, his dragnet], that is, by his manifold deceit, and gathers [[1:15|into his net|in rete suum]], that is, into hell, or into his most wicked dominion. [[1:15|for this he will be glad|Super hoc lætabitur]], for he glories in the deceiving of men.

paras.t: Propterea immolabit sagenæ suæ, id est, exercitui principum tenebrarum offeret animas, quas fefellit, torquendas. Quia in ipsis incrassata est pars ejus, id est, illorum cooperatione et tentationis subsidio plurimos sibi incorporavit, et cibus ejus electus, scilicet homines quos devorat, qui naturali dignitate cunctis mortalibus eminent.
paras.en: [[1:16|Therefore will he offer victims to his drag|Propterea immolabit sagenæ suæ]], that is, he will offer to the army of the princes of darkness the souls he has deceived, to be tormented. [[1:16|because through them his portion is made fat|Quia in ipsis incrassata est pars ejus]], that is, by their co-operation and the help of their temptation he has made very many his own, [[1:16|and his meat dainty|et cibus ejus electus]] [*electus*, "choice"], namely the men he devours, who by the dignity of their nature stand above all mortal creatures.

paras.t: Propter hoc expandit sagenam suam, id est potestatem et tentationes, vel angelos Satanæ, per quos alios capit; et semper interficere gentes non cessat, inducendo eas ad culpam mortalem, quæ vitam gratiæ perimit. Propter quod Christus disserit apud Joannem : Ille homicida erat a principio, et in veritate non stetit. Sapiens quoque testatur : Invidia diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum. Imitantur autem illum, qui sunt ex parte ipsius. Denique, Deus mortem non fecit, nec lætatur in perditione viventium; quin imo loquitur in Ezechiele, Nolo mortem morientis, sed ut convertatur et vivat.
paras.en: [[1:17|For this cause therefore he spreadeth his net|Propter hoc expandit sagenam suam]], that is, his power and temptations, or the angels of Satan, through whom he catches others; [[1:17|and will not spare continually to slay the nations|et semper interficere gentes non cessat]] [Denis reads *non cessat*, "ceaseth not"], leading them into mortal sin, which destroys the life of grace. Wherefore Christ declares in John: [[John 8:44|He was a murderer from the beginning: and he stood not in the truth|Ille homicida erat a principio, et in veritate non stetit]]. The Wise Man too bears witness: [[Wis 2:24|by the envy of the devil, death came into the world|Invidia diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum]]. [[Wis 2:25|And they follow him that are of his side|Imitantur autem illum, qui sunt ex parte ipsius]]. Moreover, [[Wis 1:13|God made not death, neither hath he pleasure in the destruction of the living|Deus mortem non fecit, nec lætatur in perditione viventium]]; nay rather, He says in Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:32|I desire not the death of him that dieth|Nolo mortem morientis]], [[Ezech 33:11|but that the wicked turn|sed ut convertatur]] [[Ezech 33:11|and live|et vivat]].
